final_synthesis:
The ozone hole was primarily caused by manufactured halocarbons like chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) and hydrochlorofluorocarbons (HCFCs), which were widely used as refrigerants, solvents, propellants, and foam-blowing agents [S1]. These compounds are broken down in the stratosphere by ultraviolet light, releasing chlorine atoms that catalytically destroy ozone molecules [S2]. The extreme cold conditions over Antarctica facilitate the formation of polar stratospheric clouds, which activate chlorine and exacerbate ozone depletion during springtime [S2].

The Montreal Protocol has successfully phased out nearly 99% of these ozone-depleting substances globally [S3]. As a result, the ozone layer is expected to recover to pre-1980 levels by approximately 2040 worldwide, with recovery over the Arctic anticipated around 2045 and in Antarctica by about 2066 [S3][S4]. However, unexpected emissions of CFC-11 from eastern China temporarily slowed this progress before decreasing again after enforcement actions were taken [S4].
